Automated evaluations yield conflicting results, with speaker similarity and automated mean opinion score predictors rating performance of GE voices inconsistently between models and human ratings. This highlights a potential blind spot in evaluation pipelines, emphasizing a need for more representative data and metrics that better capture human perceptual judgments. Our findings stress the need to include transgender, queer, and minority communities in creation of better datasets and model training.

papers.title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

papers.title: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization
papers.abstract: We transpose the Surprise-Gated Memory recipe, a frozen encoder plus a calibrated novelty signal that gates a one-shot episodic store consolidated by periodic replay, from continual visual learning to live speaker diarization. The moment-to-moment question a streaming diarizer must answer, whether an arriving voice belongs to an already-heard speaker or a new one, is a known-versus-novel decision, exactly the decision the surprise gate is built for. On a frozen fine-tuned DiariZen backbone, our online system SGM-Diar recovers 4.8 of the 9.2 diarization-error points separating a naive online baseline from the offline oracle on AMI-SDM (52%) and 1.9 of 2.3 points on VoxConverse (82%), in the end-of-meeting revisable mode, with calibration frozen on development data and transferred cross-domain without adjustment. These are single-seed runs on three AMI meetings and five VoxConverse sessions, so the ordering of conditions rather than the absolute rates is the result. Beyond error rate, we measure the gate's behaviour directly and find a coherent memory-like profile: one-shot speaker recall at 0.857, a novelty response that habituates as speakers become familiar, re-identification that is invariant to the length of intervening silence, and a false-novelty rate of 0.001. Two ablations reproduce, now on audio, the central prediction of the visual SGM work: a sliding replay window is worse than no replay at all. The memory is strictly intra-meeting and is wiped at the end, and no gradient touches the run-time system. We report SGM-Diar as a proof-of-concept and state its limitations explicitly.

papers.title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.

papers.title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

papers.title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
papers.abstract: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.

papers.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
papers.abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

papers.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
papers.abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

papers.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

papers.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
papers.abstract: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

papers.title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

papers.title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
papers.abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

papers.title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

papers.title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
papers.abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.

papers.title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

papers.title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
papers.abstract: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.

papers.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

papers.title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
papers.abstract: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.

papers.title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
papers.abstract: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.

papers.title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
papers.abstract: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.

papers.title: ANCHOR: Cluster-Grounded 5W1H Extraction via Large-Small Model Collaboration
papers.abstract: Deep semantic understanding of events requires recognizing related events and distinguishing why an event occurs from how it is carried out. 5W1H extraction provides a structured foundation for such understanding by organizing event information around six fundamental questions. However, single-event slot filling provides limited support for these distinctions. We propose ANCHOR, a cluster-grounded framework that combines a large language model (LLM) with a small language model equipped with discriminative heads for accurate 5W1H extraction. The LLM proposes candidate events and generates their initial 4W records, which guide the selection of an event cluster and the subsequent anchoring of its main event. A shared document encoder provides evidence for joint 4W refinement, and two separate sets of boundary and role-scoring heads then extract why and how under event-specific constraints, respectively. Document representations are reused across events and stages, and unsupported roles can remain empty. Following the same principles, an agent-and-skill annotation workflow constructs a benchmark of 26,110 documents from ten source corpora covering three languages and seven domains. We select nine of the resulting datasets to evaluate ANCHOR against strong baselines using four open-weight LLMs. ANCHOR achieves competitive performance. The datasets and code are available at https://github.com/revolution6575/ANCHOR-5W1H.

papers.title: PEETS: Preference-aware Embeddings with Explicit Tree Structure for Auxiliary Product Bundling
papers.abstract: Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. We present \textbf{PEETS} (\textbf{P}reference-aware \textbf{E}mbeddings with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{T}ree \textbf{S}tructure), a training-time framework for auxiliary product bundling. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.

papers.title: Post-fusion Event-aware Time-Frequency Refinement for Audio Moment Retrieval
papers.abstract: Audio Moment Retrieval (AMR) aims to locate the temporal segment within a long audio recording that semantically corresponds to a natural-language query. This task is particularly challenging because query-related audio events are often sparsely distributed and embedded in complex acoustic environments, where background sounds and acoustically similar events can easily obscure the target moments. Existing methods mainly strengthen audio-text semantic interaction to enhance the query-related information in audio frames, but seldom refine the resulting audio representations before temporal localization, limiting their ability to accurately distinguish target events from irrelevant acoustic interference. To address this issue, we propose ETR-AMR, a post-fusion event-aware time-frequency refinement framework for AMR. Specifically, an event-aware time-frequency refinement (ETR) strategy is proposed after audio-text interaction to refine fused audio frame features before temporal moment localization. ETR consists of two complementary mechanisms: time frame gating and frequency refinement. The time frame gating mechanism estimates frame-wise event relevance to emphasize query-related audio frames and suppress redundant temporal responses, while frequency refinement applies learnable time-frequency reweighting to enhance discriminative event-related frequency patterns and reduce background-dominant interference. By jointly refining fused audio frame features in the temporal and frequency domains, ETR produces more discriminative event-aware features for accurate temporal boundary prediction. Experiments on four AMR datasets demonstrate that ETR-AMR achieves superior performance compared with existing methods, especially on the high-quality CASTELLA benchmark. Duration-wise analysis further confirms the effectiveness of ETR for medium and long audio moments.

papers.title: Calibrate Once, Grow the Vocabulary: Candidate-Independent Scores for Conformal Risk Control in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary segmenters accept class names at inference. Conformal risk control can bound how often their prediction sets miss the true label, but we show that this bound breaks when names are added after calibration. On ADE20K, a threshold calibrated for 10% risk at 150 names reaches up to 15.4% risk at 845 names in released CAT-Seg models. The risk exceeds the target on every calibration split, yet the prediction sets grow far less than the target requires. In SED they instead grow larger than needed. The cause is that pruning, cross-label attention and vocabulary normalisation make each label's score depend on the other requested labels. Scores can move either way, so a threshold recalibrated at a larger vocabulary need not hold at smaller ones. We remove this dependence without training by scoring each label against a fixed reference bank of names. A label's score then stays the same when names are added, so one calibration keeps its guarantee as the vocabulary grows. The guarantee holds whatever names are added, even ones chosen per image after seeing it. On three benchmarks and five segmenters, the converted models meet the target at every vocabulary size we evaluate. For CAT-Seg and SED at alpha=10%, they use at most one more label per pixel than the released models recalibrated at the grown vocabulary. Treating names instead of images as calibration samples also bounds the miss rate of added names. If the annotated names are a random sample of the names in the calibration images, an added name's expected miss rate on those images is at most the target. For harder added names, the excess is at most their gap in mean miss rate. Applied to Grounding DINO, which splits large vocabularies into chunks, the conversion also makes inference about six times faster.

papers.title: MSAR: Next-Scale Autoregressive Forecasting for Time Series via Modular Multi-Scale Decoupling
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting underpins critical applications in finance, energy, healthcare, and transportation. Although deep models have achieved strong results, most adopt single-scale modeling or restrict multiscale processing to the input side, causing a misalignment between multiscale inputs and single-scale outputs and limiting predictive power. We introduce the Modular Scale-wise Autoregressive Framework (MSAR), a model-agnostic design that forecasts progressively across multiple temporal resolutions. MSAR offers three advantages: (1) scale-wise aligned modeling, which disentangles heterogeneous temporal patterns by aligning inputs and outputs at each scale; (2) scale-wise autoregression, where coarse-scale predictions guide finer-scale forecasting through hierarchical information flow; and (3) a modular architecture, enabling seamless integration with diverse backbones such as CNNs, MLPs, and Transformers. Extensive experiments across a broad set of datasets and forecasting models demonstrate that MSAR achieves consistent improvements in both accuracy and inference efficiency, validating the effectiveness of scale-aligned autoregression for multiscale time series forecasting. The code is available at: https://github.com/Oryxo/MSAR.

papers.title: AgentFaultBench: State-Verified Evaluation of Tool-Fault Recovery
papers.abstract: Does recovery advice help an agent finish a task after a tool fails? AgentFaultBench evaluates LangGraph and CrewAI agents performing specified tasks in an isolated GitLab installation. We inject tool errors and check both the resulting files and issues and the required reads, verification and final response. The prompt supplies the expected issue and report text, so the task tests execution rather than content generation. In the primary comparison of 1,944 planned runs, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00 and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; missing outcomes leave the latter two comparisons inconclusive. Later experiments test a revised recovery policy. GPT-4o mini improves, while Sol and Claude already complete the recoverable cases. In a separate 624-run study on six related tasks not previously used by that policy, the guided condition records 161 correct final states and one unknown outcome in 192 planned runs, versus 142/192 with neutral feedback. The gain lies between +9.90 and +10.42 pp when missing outcomes are included. Removing issue IDs gives 47/48 successes versus 46/48 with IDs; other execution information remains. A second checker agrees on 1,879 observed primary outcomes and 241 constructed test cases. No human validation was collected. The findings support testing advice against explicit recovery controls rather than assuming it helps.

papers.title: When the Bill Falls: Reusing the Old Index Defers,Never Avoids, Re-encoding in Complete Embedding-Model Migration
papers.abstract: Upgrading the embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding the corpus. Recent work reuses the old index through adapters or window re-ranking. Across sixteen model pairs on passage and code corpora, plus eleven on Natural Questions (NQ), we find three results. First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.

papers.title: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection
papers.abstract: Malware detection needs scores calibrated at a fixed false positive rate (FPR) and decisions an analyst can read: feature-based detectors give the first, large language models (LLMs) on decompiled code the second, through generated text of uncalibrated confidence. System One decision models answer a typed question about a text with a probability over its declared answers in one forward pass. We present the first evaluation of these models for Windows Portable Executable malware detection, analyze how they decide, and propose S1Mal, an ensemble on the typed answers and the embedding of CLM-8B. In an isolated virtual machine, Ghidra and capa decompose each binary, and the host renders the records into a canonical textual state, a digest of headers, imports, MITRE ATT&CK capabilities and strings, optionally with decompiled functions, without class shortcuts. Three readouts score each model on the state: A0, the probability of one verdict question; A1, 32 atomic behavioral questions weighed by gradient-boosted trees; A2, heads on the model's state embedding. S1Mal feeds gradient-boosted trees with the atomic answers and the A2 score of CLM-8B. We evaluate CLM-8B, ten open decision models and two LLMs read through logits on BODMAS temporal splits, SOREL-20M out-of-distribution malware and 14,534 matched benign files. On BODMAS, A0 wastes the static evidence: its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) spans 0.4025-0.8590 across 13 models. A1 recovers it, raising every model's AUROC by +54.61% on average; A2 lifts CLM-8B by +0.2749 to 0.9943, above a combiner on digest facts (0.9901), and reaches 0.9853-0.9948 on nine open models. S1Mal reaches 0.9946 and detects 93.47% of the malware at a realized FPR of 1.45%, and 59.15% at 0.1% FPR on the test ROC curve, against 46.59% with A2. S1Mal gives analysts calibrated decisions, each with the atomic answers behind it.

papers.title: Conic Structure of the Cross-Entropy Loss at the Final Layer and Its Absence in Rectifier Backbones
papers.abstract: Slices of the loss along lines and planes in parameter space are widely used to visualize deep networks. They often show a single basin with nearly straight walls, which raises the question of whether such a loss is a cone rounded at its apex, or a lower envelope of several cones that meet along creases. We answer this question for softmax cross-entropy at two levels of a classifier. Over the weights of an affine final layer, the loss equals a polyhedral cone plus an offset that decreases monotonically and exponentially along every ray, towards a limit in closed form. The distance at which the asymptotic wall reaches the height of the starting point, which we call the core radius, equals the mean surprisal of the classes that the direction favours, divided by the slope of the wall. Over the parameters of a rectifier backbone, the loss along a line has a kink wherever the activation pattern of a sample changes. Using the dimension theory of semialgebraic sets, we show that, along almost every line, the samples that switch at one point share an irreducible factor of their pre-activation polynomials. Under a coprimality condition, each kink therefore carries the share of one sample among $n$, so creases comparable to the slope do not form. Measurements on ResNet-18 and ResNet-56 trained on CIFAR-10 illustrate both results, with a test that bounds the size of any crease that sampled loss values can hide.

papers.title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: https://github.com/J4cksonLee/IndKnow

papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.

papers.title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

papers.title: VIVID: A Visual Harness for Agentic Video Editing
papers.abstract: Video editing requires agents to make editing decisions grounded in audiovisual observations and precise temporal localization, and to evaluate their effects in rendered outputs. General-purpose coding agents possess strong comprehension, reasoning, and code execution capabilities, while media interaction and evidence management mechanisms tailored to video tasks can further unlock their editing potential. We introduce VIVID, a visual harness that supports multiple native coding agents in video post-production without additional model training. VIVID provides tools for on-demand video inspection, audio analysis, and transcription, and preserves observations alongside their corresponding media versions and temporal coordinates. Agents can actively retrieve these observations as they reason, perform edits using their native coding and shell tools, and inspect rendered outputs to guide subsequent revisions. On AgenticVBench, comprising 100 tasks across Assembly, Repair, Sequencing, and Repurpose, Codex with VIVID achieves an average score of 58.6%, an improvement of 20.2 percentage points over native Codex. The same harness also integrates with Claude Code and OpenCode, achieving average scores of 55.1% and 37.1%, respectively, both substantially exceeding their native baselines. These results highlight VIVID's potential as a reusable visual harness for extending the capabilities of general-purpose coding agents to video editing.

papers.title: Rethinking Supervision Scaling in On-Policy Distillation: From Dense Supervision to Stochastic Horizons
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, yet the learning benefits of longer trajectories may not scale proportionally with their computational cost. We investigate how supervision utility evolves with trajectory length. Controlled experiments reveal diminishing returns from additional supervised tokens, while showing that later positions remain learnable and exhibit substantial cross-position supervision transfer. Gradient analysis further identifies shared update components across response positions and diverse position-specific residuals whose cross-rollout consistency decreases at greater depths. Motivated by these findings, we propose Stochastic Horizons On-Policy Distillation (SH-OPD), which reduces redundant supervision by randomly varying rollout horizons while preserving access to deeper response states. SH-OPD samples a shared horizon for each training batch, enabling efficient parallel generation without per-sequence horizon scheduling overhead. We characterize the resulting reweighting bias and derive a compute-reweighting trade-off under standard optimization assumptions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that SH-OPD achieves slightly higher mathematical reasoning accuracy at approximately 45% of the per-update cost of standard OPD, while maintaining competitive code generation performance at around 60% of the baseline cost. These results highlight the benefits of efficient supervision allocation across response depths.
